bib.title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering. Karpukhin, Oğuz, Min, Lewis, Wu, Edunov, Chen, Yih (Facebook AI, UW, Princeton). EMNLP 2020, pages 6769–6781 (arXiv 2004.04906).
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/sources/karpukhin-2020-dense-passage-retrieval-open-domain.pdf

COVERAGE: I read all 56,105 of 56,105 chars across every page. That includes Appendices A–D and Table 7, which come after the references. I skimmed the references only to find where the method comes from.

CLAIMS
- claim: DPR beats Lucene BM25 on top-20 and top-100 retrieval on every dataset except SQuAD, and the gap is largest at small k.
  number: NQ top-20 78.4 vs 59.1; top-100 85.4 vs 73.7. Across datasets the gain is 9–19 points at top-20.
  setup: Test sets. English Wikipedia (Dec 2018) cut into 21,015,324 passages of 100 words. Two BERT-base uncased encoders using the [CLS] vector (d=768), scored by dot product. Top-k accuracy means the top-k passages contain the answer string.
  quote: "The gap is especially large whenk is small (e.g., 78.4% vs. 59.1% for top-20 accuracy on Natural Questions)" / "outperforms a strong Lucene-BM25 system greatly by 9%-19% absolute in terms of top-20 passage retrieval accuracy" / Table 2: "None BM25 59.1 66.9 55.0 70.9 68.8 73.7 76.7 71.1 84.1 80.0" ; "Single DPR 78.4 79.4 73.2 79.8 63.2 85.4 85.0 81.4 89.1 77.2" (column order: NQ, TriviaQA, WQ, TREC, SQuAD at top-20, then the same at top-100)
  where: abstract p1; Table 2 and §5.1, p5 (chars ~18,500–20,700)
- claim: DPR also wins at top-5 on NQ.
  number: 65.2 vs 42.9
  setup: Open Natural Questions.
  quote: "outperforms BM25 by a large margin (65.2% vs. 42.9% in Top-5 accuracy)"
  where: §1, p2
- claim: In-batch negatives beat 1-of-N training with the same number of negatives, and accuracy rises with batch size. The paper says the gain comes from training on more pairs.
  number: 7 gold negatives without in-batch give 63.1 top-20; with in-batch, 69.1. In-batch with 31 and 127 negatives give 70.8 and 73.0.
  setup: NQ dev set. B questions per batch produce a B×B score matrix, giving B−1 negatives per question.
  quote: "Gold 7  42.6 63.1 78.3 / Gold 7  51.1 69.1 80.8 / Gold 31  52.1 70.8 82.1 / Gold 127  55.8 73.0 83.1" ; "accuracy consis-tently improves as the batch size grows."
  where: Table 3 and §5.2, p6
- claim: Adding one BM25 hard negative per question (shared across the batch) gives a large gain. A second one adds nothing.
  number: top-5 jumps from 55.8 to 65.8 and top-20 from 73.0 to 78.0 at batch 128. Two BM25 negatives score 76.4 top-20, against 77.3 for one.
  setup: NQ dev set. The hard negatives are passages BM25 scores highly that do not contain the answer.
  quote: "G.+BM25(1) 31+32  65.0 77.3 84.4 / G.+BM25(2) 31+64  64.5 76.4 84.0 / G.+BM25(1) 127+128  65.8 78.0 84.9" ; "adding a single BM25 negative passage improves the result substantially while adding two does not help further."
  where: Table 3, p6
- claim: In 1-of-N training, the choice of negative type matters little at k≥20.
  number: top-20 is 64.3 for random, 63.3 for BM25 and 63.1 for gold (7 negatives each)
  setup: NQ dev set, no in-batch.
  quote: "Random 7  47.0 64.3 77.8 / BM25 7  50.0 63.3 74.8" ; "does not impact the top-k accuracy much in this setting whenk≥ 20."
  where: Table 3, p6
- claim: 1,000 training examples are enough to beat BM25, and accuracy keeps rising up to 59k.
  number: 1k; 1k to 59k
  setup: NQ dev set, Figure 1.
  quote: "a dense passage retriever trained using only 1,000 ex-amples already outperforms BM25" ; "Adding more training examples (from 1k to 59k) further improves the retrieval accuracy consistently."
  where: §5.2, p6; Figure 1, p5
- claim: BM25 wins on SQuAD, and the authors give two reasons. Annotators wrote the questions while looking at the passage, so the word overlap is high. The data also comes from only 500+ articles, so it is biased.
  number: top-20 68.8 BM25 vs 63.2 DPR Single and 51.6 DPR Multi
  setup: SQuAD v1.1 test set.
  quote: "there is a high lexical overlap between passages and questions, which gives BM25 a clear advantage. Second, the data was collected from only 500+ Wikipedia articles"
  where: §5.1, p5
- claim: Qualitatively, DPR matches paraphrases ("body of water" finds Irish Sea) but misses rare salient phrases ("Thoros of Myr"), where BM25 does better.
  number: none
  setup: Table 7 examples.
  quote: "DPR excels at semantic representation, but might lack sufﬁcient capacity to represent salient phrases which appear rarely."
  where: Appendix C, p12
- claim: The hybrid takes the top 2,000 passages from BM25 and from DPR and reranks their union by a linear sum of scores. It helps on TREC and SQuAD and slightly hurts on NQ.
  number: λ=1.1. Single top-20: NQ 76.6 (DPR 78.4), TREC 85.2 (79.8), SQuAD 71.5 (63.2). Multi TREC top-100: 94.1.
  setup: Test sets. λ was tuned on dev.
  quote: "rerank the union of them using BM25(q,p) +λ· sim(q,p ) as the ranking function. We usedλ = 1.1" ; "Single DPR 78.4 79.4 73.2 79.8 63.2 ... BM25 + DPR 76.6 79.8 71.0 85.2 71.5 83.8 84.5 80.5 92.7 81.3" ; "Multi ... BM25 + DPR 78.0 79.9 74.7 88.5 66.2 83.9 84.4 82.3 94.1 78.6"
  where: §5 and Table 2, p5
- claim: Dense search is about 40 times faster per query than Lucene BM25. Building the dense index is far slower, though.
  number: 995.0 vs 23.7 questions/s. Embedding takes 8.8 h on 8 GPUs, the FAISS build takes 8.5 h, and the Lucene build takes about 30 min.
  setup: Intel Xeon E5-2698 v4, 512GB RAM, top-100 per question. FAISS uses HNSW on CPU with 512 neighbours per node, efConstruction 200 and search depth 128. BM25 is measured per CPU thread from a file index, so the comparison is not like for like.
  quote: "processing 995.0 questions per second, returning top 100 pas-sages per question. In contrast, BM25/Lucene ... processes 23.7 questions per second per CPU thread." ; "taking roughly 8.8 hours on 8 GPUs. However, building the FAISS index on 21-million vectors on a single server takes 8.5 hours. ... takes only about 30 minutes in total."
  where: §5.4 and footnote 10, p6–7
- claim: Better retrieval gives better end-to-end QA, with state of the art on 4 of 5 datasets.
  number: NQ EM 41.5 (DPR) vs 32.6 (BM25) vs 33.3 (ORQA)
  setup: BERT-base reader over the top-k passages, scored by exact match.
  quote: "DPR 41.5 56.8 34.6 25.9 29.8" ; "BM25 32.6 52.4 29.9 24.9 38.1" ; "(41.5% vs. 33.3%)"
  where: Table 4, p7; §1
- claim: The similarity function and loss matter little. L2 is about the same as dot product, both beat cosine, and triplet loss is close to NLL.
  number: top-20 78.1 for DP/NLL, 76.1 for L2/NLL, 77.2 for DP/Triplet
  setup: NQ dev set. These use better hyperparameters than Table 3.
  quote: "DP NLL 44.9 66.8 78.1 85.0Triplet 41.6 65.0 77.2 84.5" ; "L2 performs compara-ble to dot product, and both of them are superior to cosine."
  where: §5.2; Table 6, p12
- claim: Distant supervision (taking the top BM25 passage that contains the answer as the positive) costs only about 1 point.
  number: 77.1 vs 78.1 top-20
  setup: NQ dev set.
  quote: "Gold 44.9 66.8 78.1 85.0 / Dist. Sup. 43.9 65.3 77.1 84.4"
  where: Table 5, p12
- claim: A model trained only on NQ transfers to other datasets, losing 3–5 points against fine-tuned models while still beating BM25.
  number: top-20 69.9/86.3 vs 75.0/89.1 for WQ/TREC, with BM25 at 55.0/70.9
  setup: Trained on NQ only.
  quote: "3-5 points loss from the best performing ﬁne-tuned model in top-20 retrieval accuracy (69.9/86.3 vs. 75.0/89.1 for WebQuestions and TREC, respectively), while still greatly outperforming the BM25 baseline (55.0/70.9)."
  where: §5.2, p6
- claim: Main training settings.
  number: batch 128 plus 1 BM25 negative; up to 40 epochs on large datasets and 100 on small; learning rate 1e-5
  quote: "batch size of128 and one additional BM25 negative passage per question ... 40 epochs for large datasets (NQ, TriviaQA, SQuAD) and 100 epochs for small datasets (TREC, WQ), with a learning rate of 10−5 using Adam"
  where: §5, p5
- claim: Retrieving fewer passages costs little accuracy.
  number: k=10 gives 40.8 vs 41.5 EM on NQ, and k=50 is optimal
  quote: "k = 10 leads to only marginal loss in exact match accuracy (40.8 vs. 41.5 EM on NQ)"
  where: §6.2, p7

LIMITS: Results cover factoid QA over a single Wikipedia snapshot only, with 100-word passages and BERT-base encoders. Accuracy means the answer string appears in the passage, which is a proxy for relevance rather than a judgment. The hybrid is a simple linear sum with one λ tuned on dev, and it does not always beat DPR alone. RRF was not tried. The speed comparison sets FAISS HNSW in memory against Lucene per thread on a file index. Index build cost is high and the paper does not cover index refresh. The authors concede that SQuAD is biased and that dense retrieval misses rare salient phrases. Since 2020 the model has been overtaken by ANCE-style iterative hard negatives, which the paper itself cites (Xiong 2020a), and by later embedders. Dense retrieval's out-of-domain weakness is shown only through the light NQ→WQ/TREC transfer test.

BUILDS ON: BERT (Devlin et al., 2019); the Siamese dual encoder (Bromley et al., 1994); in-batch negatives (Yih et al., 2011; Henderson et al., 2017; Gillick et al., 2019); ORQA/ICT (Lee et al., 2019); BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009); FAISS (Johnson et al., 2017); DrQA preprocessing (Chen et al., 2017); 100-word passages (Wang et al., 2019); metric learning (Kulis, 2013); triplet loss (Burges et al., 2005). Concurrent work: REALM (Guu et al., 2020) and ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020).

CODE: None in the paper. The loss (Eq. 2, p3) is the negative log of softmax(sim(q,p+)) over the positive plus n negatives, with sim(q,p) = EQ(q)⊺EP(p). In-batch scoring is "S = QPT is a (B×B) ma-trix of similarity scores" (p3–4). The code is released at https://github.com/facebookresearch/DPR.

FIGURES: Figure 1, p5: "Retriever top-k accuracy with different numbers of training examples used in our dense passage retriever vs BM25 ... Our DPR trained using 1,000 examples already outperforms BM25." The curves show sample efficiency and the narrowing gap as k grows faster than prose can. Table 7 (p13) is not a figure but shows side by side where each retriever fails, and it makes a good teaching example.

PROBLEMS: The extraction is clean apart from merged table rows ("...77.2BM25 + DPR"), which I re-read using the column headers. Table 3's in-batch check marks did not come through, so I took in-batch status from the row order and the text. One inconsistency I left unresolved: §6.2 reports joint training at "39.8 EM" with no split named, and the main DPR NQ figure (41.5) is a test score, while Appendix D gives the same 39.8 "on NQ dev as in our regular reader model". The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
